kurz: Why profit alone says nothing about value creation, and why only the gap between return on capital and cost of capital shows whether growth creates or destroys value.

bloecke.md:
A company employs capital to generate cash flows. It ties up money in machinery, inventories, receivables and acquired companies and earns a return on it. Whether value is created in the process depends on the gap between this return and the return the same capital would earn elsewhere at the same risk. The size of the profit is not the deciding factor.

This gap is called the **spread**, and value is created only through it. It results from two figures, the return on capital [[Return on invested capital (ROIC)|ROIC]] and the cost of capital [[Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)|WACC]]. How the WACC is estimated is covered in the lesson on the cost of capital. Here it is treated as a given hurdle.

bloecke.formel: ROIC = NOPAT / invested capital,   NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − s)
bloecke.erklaerung: Numerator and denominator must relate to the same level of capital. A return before financing costs is therefore set against capital that comprises both debt and equity. Only then can the figure be compared with the WACC.
variablen: operating profit after tax, before interest
interest-bearing debt plus equity, excluding excess cash
bloecke.beispiel: EBIT €100 million, s = 30%: NOPAT = €70 million. With €350 million of invested capital, this gives a ROIC of 20.0%.

bloecke.md:
## How numerator and denominator are formed

No interest is deducted in the numerator, because its price is already contained in the WACC. If you deduct it as well and still compare with the WACC, the cost of debt is counted twice.

For the tax rate in Germany, 15% corporation tax (Section 23(1) KStG, Corporation Tax Act) and the 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it add up to 15.825%. In addition there is trade tax (Gewerbesteuer), which is the base rate (Steuermesszahl) of 3.5% (Section 11(2) GewStG, Trade Tax Act) multiplied by the municipal multiplier (Hebesatz, Section 16 GewStG). With a multiplier of 400%, that comes to 14%, making just under 30% in total. In cities with a high multiplier, the rate is closer to 33%. Since July 2025 the law has laid down that corporation tax will fall to 14% from 2028 and then by one percentage point a year until it reaches 10% from 2032 (Section 23(1) KStG). This increases future NOPAT figures for tax reasons alone.

The denominator can be built from two sides, as interest-bearing debt plus equity or as fixed assets plus working capital. Both routes must give the same result. Excess cash is excluded because the interest earned on it is not contained in EBIT. The same applies to equity investments that are not needed for operations.

Value is created only if ROIC is greater than WACC. If ROIC is below it, every additional euro invested destroys value, and growth accelerates this destruction of value. If ROIC is exactly as high as WACC, growth is value-neutral. The company then gets bigger, but its value does not rise.

## Two companies with the same profit

Both model companies earn EBIT of €100 million, pay 30% tax and arrive at NOPAT of €70 million. Both retain a quarter of it and are valued at a cost of capital of 9%, which is roughly the average for German companies. They differ only in the capital tied up. The specialist machine builder needs €350 million for its profit, the supplier €1,000 million.

bloecke.titel: Same profit and cash flow with almost double the value (illustrative calculation)

bloecke.md: Both companies pay out €52.5 million in the coming year and are nevertheless worth different amounts. The reason is in the table two rows above. The same €17.5 million of reinvestment brings 5% growth at the specialist machine builder and 1.75% at the supplier. How much growth a reinvestment generates therefore depends on ROIC.

bloecke.titel: Reconciliation from NOPAT to residual income at the supplier (€m)
bloecke.unter: Only the cost of capital on €1,000 million of capital tied up shows that the supplier earns €20 million a year less than its capital costs. For the specialist machine builder, the same position shows a surplus of €38.5 million.

bloecke.formel: EVA = NOPAT − WACC × invested capital = (ROIC − WACC) × invested capital
bloecke.erklaerung: Residual income is the profit after deducting the cost of all the capital employed. It thus takes into account what the income statement leaves out. Equity also has a cost, but it is booked there without any interest charge.
variablen: Economic Value Added, also known as residual income
cost of capital in euros, the hurdle for the year

bloecke.md: The sum of all future EVA, each discounted, gives the market value added. This is the amount a buyer can pay over and above the invested capital. In the example, the calculation works out exactly. For the specialist machine builder, €38.5 million growing by 5% a year and discounted at 9% gives 38.5 / (0.09 − 0.05) = 963 million. This amount corresponds exactly to the difference between the value of operations and invested capital. For the supplier it is −20 / (0.09 − 0.0175) = −276 million. The income statement does not point to this difference anywhere.

## Growth and reinvestment

Earning more requires more capital tied up, for example for new plant, larger inventories, longer receivable periods or acquisitions. How much growth a retained euro makes possible is determined by ROIC. This gives the central relationship of this lesson. In the steady state it holds exactly and not merely approximately.

bloecke.erklaerung: Growth is the product of the return on capital and the share of profit retained, and it cannot be set independently of them. Any forecast that assumes high growth with a low ROIC and a high payout contradicts this equation.
variablen: sustainable growth of NOPAT and capital, without new capital from outside
bloecke.beispiel: ROIC 20%, a quarter of NOPAT reinvested: 20% × 0.25 = 5% growth. Conversely, a company that wants to grow permanently by 6% with a ROIC of 8% must retain three quarters of NOPAT, so that only a quarter is left for the owners.

bloecke.md:
At the specialist machine builder, 25% of €70 million, that is €17.5 million, stays in the company. As a result, capital grows from €350 million to €367.5 million. In the following year NOPAT is 20% × 367.5 = €73.5 million, exactly 5% more.

At the supplier, the same €17.5 million stays in the company, and capital grows from €1,000 million to €1,017.5 million. In the following year NOPAT is 7% × 1,017.5 = €71.2 million, that is 1.75% more. Here the same capital employed brings only just over a third of the increase in earnings.

bloecke.erklaerung: The numerator is free cash flow, that is NOPAT less the part that remains tied up in the company for growth. Growth therefore acts in two places, because it shrinks the denominator and at the same time reduces the numerator. Which effect prevails depends solely on the relationship between ROIC and WACC.
bloecke.beispiel: Supplier: 70 × (1 − 1.75 / 7) / (0.09 − 0.0175) = 52.5 / 0.0725 = €724 million. Without growth and with a full payout, the result is 70 / 0.09 = €778 million. Here growth therefore costs €54 million.

bloecke.titel: Value of the business by growth and return on capital (€m)
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with the formula above for NOPAT of €70 million and a WACC of 9%, varying growth and ROIC; with ROIC equal to WACC, the value stays the same across all growth rates.

bloecke.md: The chart shows three relationships. First, without growth all four cases are worth the same, because their NOPAT is set at the same level and only the capital tied up to earn it differs. Return on capital alone therefore does not change the value of the business; it only takes effect together with growth. Second, with ROIC equal to WACC the series is flat, no matter how fast the company grows. Third, below the cost of capital the sign reverses. There, shrinking is worth more than growing, and the most sensible contribution a management board can make is to return capital instead of tying it up again.

Revenue and profit growth are firmly embedded in management board pay and in analyst models, returns on capital much less often. This explains some of the takeovers that turned out in hindsight to destroy value. An acquisition almost always increases absolute profit, because acquired companies rarely earn nothing at all. Whether it creates value, however, depends on the return on the purchase price paid and not on the return on the book value of the company acquired. The goodwill paid therefore belongs in invested capital.

## Current level of the cost of capital

The KPMG Cost of Capital Study surveys the cost of capital applied in practice at around 300 mostly German companies, including about two thirds of the DAX 40 constituents. The 2025 edition reports an average WACC of 8.5%, after 8.2% in the previous year, as well as an average cost of equity of 9.7% and an average levered beta of 1.03. The German participants used, on average, a risk-free rate of 2.5% and a market risk premium of 6.7%. With these averages, the CAPM gives 2.5 + 1.03 × 6.7 = 9.4%. The 9.7%, by contrast, is the mean of the costs of equity that each company determines with its own assumptions, and so it cannot be recalculated exactly.

The base rate (Basiszins) of 2.5% is now out of date. Ten-year German federal bonds (Bunds) yielded around 3.5% on 18 September 2026, close to their highest level since 2011. Hurdles are therefore likely to be higher in 2026, so that fewer companies clear them. For valuations under IDW S1 (the valuation standard of the German Institute of Public Auditors), the relevant rate is in any case the base rate derived from the Bundesbank's yield curve and not the daily yield.

bloecke.titel: Cost of capital by sector in Germany (%)
bloecke.unter: KPMG Cost of Capital Study 2025. The same 8% return on capital creates value in the real estate sector and destroys it in the technology sector. A ROIC figure is therefore only meaningful together with the cost of capital hurdle of its sector.

bloecke.md:
## Distortions of ROIC

ROIC is an accounting figure, and accounting reflects capital tied up only incompletely. Four distortions work in the same direction. They make the denominator look too small and ROIC therefore too high.

bloecke.titel: Four systematic distortions of invested capital
zeilen: Book value far below replacement value
too high, and rising for no operational reason
Check gross fixed assets and any investment backlog
Investment does not appear on the balance sheet
far too high for software and pharma

Research costs are always expensed under IAS 38 and the HGB (Commercial Code); development costs must be capitalised under IAS 38 if the criteria are met, and may optionally be capitalised under Section 248(2) HGB; as a substitute, treat R&D as capitalised over several years
often left out, as “ROIC ex goodwill”
Include the purchase price paid when assessing value creation
off balance sheet before IFRS 16, often still expensed under the HGB
too high for retail, logistics and airlines
Since 2019, IFRS 16 has capitalised right-of-use assets; adjust HGB figures and older series accordingly

bloecke.md: Return on equity (ROE) can be raised through borrowing, and also through share buybacks that reduce balance sheet equity without the business earning a single euro more. ROIC, by contrast, is largely insensitive to this, because it carries debt and equity together in the denominator. ROE should therefore always be looked at together with ROIC and the equity ratio.

## How long a positive spread lasts

A positive spread attracts competitors, because capital flows to where it earns more. In economic terms, the return must therefore converge on the cost of capital in the long run. How quickly this happens is disputed and depends heavily on the business model. Expressed in figures, this is the question of the economic moat.

Two things follow for valuation. A ROIC that stays far above the WACC over the long term is a strong assumption and not an observation. It has to be justified and must not go into the terminal value without comment. In addition, company growth is empirically neither easy to predict nor stable over longer periods, and forecasts beyond three to five years contain little information.

In the WACC, the cost of debt carries the factor (1 − s), because interest is tax-deductible. In Germany, however, this applies only to a limited extent.

First, Section 8 no. 1 letter a GewStG adds a quarter of interest expenses back to trade income (Gewerbeertrag), to the extent that the total of all financing components under Section 8 no. 1 GewStG, before the one-quarter factor is applied, exceeds the allowance of €200,000. Of the combined rate of around 29.8%, the effective interest saving is more in the order of 26%.

Second, the interest barrier (Zinsschranke) under Section 4h EStG (Income Tax Act) in conjunction with Section 8a KStG limits the deduction of net interest expense to 30% of EBITDA for tax purposes once the exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of three million euros is exceeded. For highly leveraged structures, the tax advantage should therefore not be applied across the board. If it is already included in the WACC, it must on no account also appear in the cash flows.

1. Take EBIT from the income statement and adjust it for clearly identified one-off effects.
2. Multiply by (1 − tax rate). The group tax rate is given in the notes.
3. Build invested capital from the liabilities side, that is equity plus interest-bearing financial liabilities including leases, minus excess cash.
4. Use the average of the start and end of the year, so that an acquisition does not distort the picture.
5. Put five to ten years side by side, because a single year's figure says almost nothing.
6. Compare ROIC with the sector hurdle and multiply the difference by invested capital. The result is EVA in euros.

mitnehmen: Value creation is decided by the gap between ROIC and WACC, multiplied by the capital tied up, and not by the size of the profit.
Growth only amplifies the effect of this gap: above the cost of capital it creates value, below it accelerates the destruction of value, and with ROIC equal to WACC it has no effect.
Because g = ROIC × reinvestment rate, a forecast of high growth with a low return on capital implies that only a small part of NOPAT is left for the owners.

Many companies report a ROIC or ROCE, each with its own definition; for an assessment it is calculated on a uniform basis and adjusted for goodwill, leases, research expense and depreciated old assets, because all four distortions make the figure look too favourable.
A permanently positive spread is an assumption about future competition and not a constant, and justifying it is the essential content of a quality analysis.

begriffe.text: Return on all the capital tied up in the business, calculated as NOPAT divided by invested capital. ROIC is independent of financing and can therefore be compared directly with WACC.
Operating profit after tax but before interest, calculated as EBIT times (1 − tax rate). It is attributable to all providers of capital together.
Interest-bearing debt plus equity, excluding excess cash and non-operating assets. From the assets side, the same amount results as fixed assets plus working capital.
Economic Value Added or residual income, calculated as NOPAT minus the cost of capital, which equals WACC times invested capital. The present value of all future EVA is the market value added.
Share of NOPAT that stays in the company as net investment. Multiplied by ROIC, it gives sustainable growth.
